scope.basis: physics/length-weight.csv: fitted field studies (n 117 to 2769) of fishery-caught flying fish, lengths about 15 to 30 cm
scope.note: The 1 male-only row (Hirundichthys affinis, b = 2.208) is EXCLUDED and named: including it would widen the band to 2.21. Length types differ across rows (SL, FL, TL) and the FishBase page does not show the references. Eighteen further rows with b exactly 3.000 and n of 2 to 6 are unverified estimates and are not used. When the mass exponent is IMPLIED against the reference specimen rather than committed from a fit, it is not evaluated at a length ratio inside [0.905, 1.105]: an implied exponent is ln(X/X_ref) / ln(L/L_ref) against the single reference specimen (Cypselurus hiraii, Park and Choi 2010 Table 1 model L3, SL 0.203 m), so the denominator approaches zero as L approaches L_ref and ordinary specimen variation is amplified without limit. About 1% relative uncertainty in L against the studio's 0.1 decision band means the comparison carries no information until |ln(L/L_ref)| >= 0.1, i.e. a length ratio outside [0.905, 1.105]. Measured in the real siblings: L1 (ratio 1.0099) implied a v_min exponent of -1.43 and L2 (1.0296) -3.86 against a target of 0.5, and model N (0.9951) -60.8, so accepted laws fired red on unedited wild-type flying fish (blind evaluator, 2026-11-01).
applies_to: a mass exponent fitted over a size range: a length-weight regression, or a design that commits mass_exponent
excludes: an exponent IMPLIED against the single reference specimen at a length ratio inside [0.905, 1.105]: ln(L/L_ref) is then too small to carry an exponent (about 1% relative uncertainty in L against the studio's 0.1 band), so the number says nothing about the fitted band. Commit mass_exponent from a fit instead. The real Park and Choi siblings L1 (ratio 1.0099), L2 (1.0296) and model N (0.9951) fell here and came back red against this law (blind evaluator, 2026-11-01).
